name: waymark
short: Durable background jobs for Python on top of Postgres. Workflows are compiled once and survive restarts and crashes.
what: waymark lets you write background workflows as ordinary async Python that keep going through server restarts, task crashes and long jobs. It needs only Postgres. Workflows are compiled to bytecode for a durable virtual machine in a Rust runtime, so your code is never replayed and doesn't have to be deterministic. It has per-call retries and timeouts, parallel fan-out, durable sleep, cron schedules and a built-in webapp.
who: Python developers already on Postgres who want durable jobs without running a separate broker. The author says not to use it in production yet. Skip it if you need under 100 ms task handling or more than about 10k actions coordinated at once.
needs: Python and a package manager (the README uses uv)
Node.js and npm, plus Rust, only if you build from source

steps.title: Install
steps.text: One Python package holds the client and server binaries.

steps.title: Write actions and a workflow
steps.text: Actions are plain async functions marked `@action`. The workflow is a class marked `@workflow` with an async `run()` method that calls them. The README's example fetches users and sends welcome emails in parallel.

steps.title: Run the node against your database
steps.text: The webapp is then on http://localhost:24119.
steps.code:
export WAYMARK_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/waymark
export WAYMARK_HTTP_ENABLED=true  # the webapp, on http://localhost:24119
uv run waymark-executor

steps.title: Start a workflow
steps.text: From any Python process. The run is queued to Postgres and executed by the node, not inline in your web server.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Follow the Quickstart at waymark.sh/python/quickstart, then give one action a retry policy with `self.run_action(..., retry=RetryPolicy(attempts=5, backoff_seconds=10), timeout=timedelta(minutes=2))`.

watch: The README says not to use it in production yet. The spec changes quickly and there is no backwards compatibility before 1.0.0.
Workflow code must use supported patterns. Some patterns still slip past the compiler; they are listed under known issues in the docs.
It runs on Postgres alone, so very high job volumes will eventually tax your database.
